## Overview

The Rikbaktsa are an Indigenous group from the Mato Grosso region of Brazil. They live in the Amazon rain forest of northwest Mato Grosso, in the basin of the Juruena River. Their traditional territory extended from the Papagaio River to the Augusto Falls on the upper Tapajós River, and was bounded by the Aripuanã and Arinos rivers. Today they have rights to the Erikbaktsa, Japuíra, and Escondido Indigenous Lands. As of 2001, there were 909 Rikbaktsa people. Their language, called Rikbaktsa or Erikbaktsa, is a Macro-Gê language. Their culture includes oral storytelling, myth, ritualized hunting, fishing, gathering and agriculture, traditional music, body paint, feather ornaments, flute-playing, and ceremonies connected with maize and forest clearing.

## Material culture

### Clothing & dress

The sources mention traditional dress as a unifying element in the face of contact with the outside world. Ceremonies often involve body paint and feather ornaments.

### Architecture

 They mention domestic groups, villages, and a men's house where boys may learn ceremonies, myths, traditional medicine, and flute-playing.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

 They state that boys learn to make and use their own bow and arrows by age eight or ten, and that the Rikbaktsa use wooden plugs to enlarge their earlobes.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Rikbaktsa body adornment includes enlarged earlobes made with wooden plugs, a practice associated with the name Orelhas de Pau, or “Wooden Ears.” Boys traditionally had their noses pierced during the ceremony of the maize at age eleven or twelve, when they received a second name. Girls traditionally had their noses pierced around age 12 and could have their faces tattooed in a ceremony decided by their fathers. Ceremonies may also involve body paint and feather ornaments.

## Music & performance

Music is part of Rikbaktsa ceremonial life and has served as a unifying element during contact with the outside world. Ceremonies often involve flute-playing of traditional songs, and boys may learn flute-playing in the men's house after receiving their second name. Music occurs together with body paint, feather ornaments, and the performance of mythical stories and recent fights.

The sources identify the January green maize ceremony and the May forest-clearing ceremony as the two largest ceremonies. Hunting, fishing, gathering, and agriculture are ritualized through ceremonies held throughout the year.

## Dance & theatre

 They state that ceremonies can include the performance of mythical stories and recent fights.

## Festivals & rituals

The two largest Rikbaktsa ceremonies are the January green maize ceremony and the May forest-clearing ceremony. Agriculture is central to the timing of tribal life, and hunting, fishing, gathering, and agriculture are ritualized through ceremonies throughout the year. These ceremonies may involve body paint, feather ornaments, flute-playing of traditional songs, and performances of mythical stories and recent fights.

Rikbaktsa boys receive a child name at birth. Between three and five years old, a boy begins hunting with his father and learning about hunting, animals, and local geography. By age eight or ten, he can make and use his own bow and arrows. At age eleven or twelve, after mastering the bow and arrow, his nose is pierced during the ceremony of the maize and he receives a second name. Traditionally, around age 14 or 15, a boy capable of hunting large animals and knowledgeable about ceremonies had his ears pierced in a ritual celebration. This marked the transition to manhood and eligibility for marriage, but the rite is now obsolete.

Girls traditionally had their noses pierced around age 12 and took “forest medicine” to reduce the pain expected during later childbirth. Face tattooing after nose piercing traditionally marked womanhood and eligibility for marriage, but this rite is no longer practiced. Following nose piercing, possible tattooing, and marriage, a woman could receive a new name replacing her child name. Shortly after the corresponding male rituals, or after marriage, a young man receives his third, adult name.

## Foodways

The Rikbaktsa consider themselves hunter-gatherers rather than farmers, although agriculture is central to the timing of tribal life. Each residence generally produces and consumes its own food. Traditional subsistence includes hunting, fishing, gathering, and slash-and-burn agriculture. Planting fields of ½–2 hectare are cleared by fire every 2 or 3 years, while old fields are generally left fallow and eventually retaken by the forest.

The Rikbaktsa regularly plant rice, cassava, maize, yams, beans, cotton, urucu, bananas, peanuts, sugarcane, and pumpkin. They also plant limes, oranges, tangerines, pineapple, mangoes, and other fruits on occasion. Agricultural rituals and the January green maize ceremony connect food production with the ritual calendar.

## Oral tradition & literature

Oral storytelling and myth are important to the Rikbaktsa. Their oral histories, geographic references in myths, and detailed knowledge of nearby flora and fauna suggest a long connection with their traditional lands. Ceremonies may include performances of mythical stories and recent fights.

Rikbaktsa belief includes reincarnation. Future incarnations depend on the life a person led: virtuous people may be reincarnated as human beings or night monkeys, while villainous people may be reincarnated as dangerous animals such as jaguars or poisonous snakes. The Rikbaktsa believe that all organisms were once human and were transformed into animals permanently. They state that the Asirik association, created in 1995, works to provide a more unified voice for Rikbaktsa people and to interact with external agencies.

## Language & religion

The Rikbaktsa language is also called Erikbaktsa. It is described as a Macro-Gê language, while the separate language article states that it forms its own branch of the Macro-Gê languages or is a language isolate. It is also spelled Aripaktsa, Erikbatsa, or Erikpatsa and is known ambiguously as Canoeiro. Most Rikbaktsa speak both Rikbaktsa and Portuguese. Younger people tend to speak Portuguese more frequently and fluently, while older people generally struggle with Portuguese and use it mainly with non-indigenous Brazilians. Rikbaktsa is a subject-object-verb language, and word endings indicate the gender of the speaker.

The sources describe Rikbaktsa beliefs rather than a named religious affiliation. Sickness is understood as resulting from breaking taboos, spells, or poisoning by enemies. Traditional medicine uses plant matter and ritual purification.
